extracted.intended_audience: computer-science students and authors writing technical/academic term papers and expository prose (Stanford CS class audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing clear, readable, and correct technical/expository prose (term papers, lectures, and technical exposition), with specific rules on grammar, punctuation, notation, example sequencing, and how to use automated style/readability tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid symbol clutter and ambiguous notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not crowd the page with too many similar symbols (e.g., Hi, Hj, Hj').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either write out the concept in words (e.g., 'each Hi is ...') or invent another name when you will use a construct repeatedly; avoid constructs that create ambiguity or confusion when primed/modified forms are used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use correct genitive (possessive) punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use an apostrophe for the genitive (possessive) case (e.g., "Hi's descendants").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructs like "Hi S descendants" that omit the apostrophe and confuse meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenate compound adjectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Hyphenate adjectival compounds that modify a noun ('one-vertex path' not 'one vertex path').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a hyphen to signal that the compound modifies the noun as a single unit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer precise prepositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose prepositions that convey the intended relation (e.g., 'vertex at distance d' rather than 'vertex of distance d').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small prepositional choices affect clarity; prefer 'at' for indicating distance relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include spacing and punctuation around references
rubrics_metrics.description: Put appropriate spaces and punctuation around references (e.g., 'using 4.3 (below) we derive ...' rather than '4.3(below)').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure typographic spacing so line breaks and inline references don't run words together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect logical/proof ordering
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use a lemma or theorem before it is proved; ensure the reader sees results only after prerequisites are established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using an unproved result earlier can make readers suspect circular reasoning or a 'fast one'; structure proofs so dependencies are clear and respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use ties/nonbreaking spaces to keep related words together
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ties (nonbreaking spaces) to prevent line breaks from splitting phrases that should remain together (e.g., between 'e' and 'is', or after 'dominates' in 'v dominates x').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This keeps line breaks from interrupting or distorting the message; tie words that form a unit you don't want separated by a break.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ambiguous words used in multiple senses
rubrics_metrics.description: Be wary of words that can be interpreted in different senses in the same context (e.g., 'left' as direction vs past tense; 'plane' meaning airplane vs complex plane).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose wording or rephrase to disambiguate when the same word might cause confusion in multiple senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence examples to build upon one another
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer a sequence of examples that build on each other over a set of unrelated examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A progressive sequence of illustrations helps learning; the lecture praised Haddad and Schiffer's sequence of illustrations as a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'that' for restrictive (defining) clauses, 'which' for nonrestrictive
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat 'that' as the defining/restrictive relative pronoun and 'which' as non-defining/non-restrictive; enclose non-defining clauses between commas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The lawn mower that is broken is in the garage.' (restrictive) vs 'The lawn mower, which is broken, is in the garage.' (nonrestrictive). Follow Rule 3: enclose parenthetic expressions between commas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical substitution rule for which/that
rubrics_metrics.description: If you can substitute 'that' for 'which' and it sounds all right, do so (Strunk & White / Leslie Lamport rule).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This simple test helps decide which to use in everyday expository prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Which/that guidance applies mainly to everyday expository prose
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'which' vs 'that' rule is intended for everyday, expository, 'shirt-sleeve' prose, not necessarily for literary prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors may violate the rule in literary writing for effect; the rule is primarily for clarity in expository texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and micro-choices affect readership
rubrics_metrics.description: Tiny choices (like which vs that) influence tone; many small wrong choices reduce reader attention and commitment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for consistent micro-decisions to maximize readership; readers who don't have to read will stop if tone is off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use calisthenic exercises selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: Verse, prosody, and rhetorical-term exercises can train writing skills but are primarily exercises (not ends in themselves).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some exercises (e.g., prosodic form work) are valuable; avoid exercises that are not profitable for your goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability grade-level metrics: understand basis and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Readability programs compute a 'grade' from average words/sentence and average syllables/word via linear regression against judged grade levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may aim to minimize grade level but avoid overdoing it; the metrics are superficial and should prompt re-reading rather than be followed rigidly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use automated style outputs as diagnostic, not authoritative
rubrics_metrics.description: Style programs provide extra parameters (average sentence length, percent too short/long, sentence-starters, sentence-type frequencies, POS percentages, passive voice flags, etc.) but their analyses are superficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these outputs to re-read and reconsider prose; they can suggest problems (e.g., too much passive voice) even if the program misclassifies musical or legitimate long sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of program quirks (expletive classification, passive detection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some tools classify any sentence beginning with 'It ...' or 'There ...' as 'expletive' and mark sentences as passive if a passive verb appears anywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret such flags cautiously and in context—tools may overflag or misinterpret stylistic choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction filters flag 'suspect' words/phrases and suggest alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs like diction maintain lists of questionable words/phrases ('gratuitous', 'number of', 'due to', 'very', 'literally', 'in fact', etc.) and invite the writer to find alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users reportedly accept ~50% of suggestions; consider but don't accept blindly—mathematical usages (e.g., 'due to' in attribution) may be appropriate despite general editorial preferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous intensifiers like 'very'
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'very' unless you would happily substitute a stronger colloquial (advice: try replacing 'very' with 'damn' as a test).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps tighten prose and avoid weak intensifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strive for clarity, coherence, accuracy, and concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Good writing must be clear, coherent, accurate, and concise; concision is especially important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut unnecessary words/phrases; Pascal quoted: longer first drafts result from lack of time to make them shorter; editing down improves clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Answer more questions than you raise
rubrics_metrics.description: A hallmark of good writing is that it resolves readers' likely questions rather than creating new ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague references or incomplete information that prompts unnecessary reader questions; be explicit about what you're referring to.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delete unnecessary verbs/phrases ('he has heard', 'one of the most encouraging signs is the fact')
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove wordy constructions that add no information; rephrase 'he has heard one of the largest paper manufacturers...' to 'one of the largest paper manufacturers...' or 'We remove the spaces because...' instead of 'The reason for removing the spaces is that...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for and cut filler phrases to increase directness and concision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer short sentences; use periods over semicolons
rubrics_metrics.description: Cut long sentences into shorter ones where possible; semicolons slow pace and evoke '19th-century mustiness'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use semicolons only when separated clauses have a very close relationship; often a period is better for readability and pace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conversational idioms and informal filler in technical writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid conversational openings ('Anyway, ...'), vague qualifiers ('pretty straightforward'), and awkward phrases ('again iterate through') in technical/expository writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such idioms lower formality and precision; prefer smoother, more exact expressions in papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep the grammatical subject near the beginning; prefer S–V–O
rubrics_metrics.description: Many hard-to-read sentences separate subject and verb by many words; favor subject–verb–object order to improve readability and reduce passive voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopting S–V–O style reduces passive constructions and improves clarity; move the subject forward in the sentence when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read text aloud to detect repetition and awkward phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading aloud helps spot overuse of words ('this', 'they', 'just', 'then'), repetition, and other rhythm problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use aloud-reading as an editing technique to find repeated words and places where sentences drag or sound awkward.
